subtopic: SITTING RESUMED
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in considering the amendment that was moved by the Minister of National Defence with the unanimous consent of the committee, I think there are one or two comments which should be made, because in addition to the contentious point with respect to a review that would be made upon application to the railways there is also one other very important part which was also left out of the amendment moved by the Minister of National Defence, and on which there was no contention.
While I certainly do not wish to take a lot of time discussing this bill any further, because we have been through it a number of times, I wonder whether the minister would be willing to accept an amendment to his amendment and include a subclause dealing with a crown representative before the Transport Commission whenever the commission was considering a matter related to the
January 26, 1967

revenues and costs of a railway company under the jurisdiction of parliament. This particular subclause reads:
Where in any proceedings before the commission under this act the matter of the revenues or costs of a railway company under the jurisdiction or parliament is under investigation, any minister of the crown in right of Canada may cause representations to be made thereon to the commission by persons having knowledge or costing principles or matters that appear to such minister to be relevant to the determination or railway revenues and costs.
It seems to me that it would be appropriate to include this wording as subsection 4 of section 470 in clause 74. At present section 470 contains three subsections and I do not think that the fourth subsection as proposed would be in contradiction of them. In fact it would replace the provision in which the Minister of Transport, and I presume the Minister of Finance or even the Minister of Agriculture may have a keen interest, to ensure that the cost formula used could be adequately investigated. There have been far too many cases in the past when the only really competent cost accountants and analysts who appeared before the Board of Transport Commissioners were from the railways. There have been only one or two important exceptions when experts in this field have been brought in to challenge the costing formula and other factors advanced by the railway. The Crowsnest pass rates, and revenues from those rates, are examples that come to my mind. The minister knows that these rates were challenged before the MacPherson Royal Commission and that the provinces of Manitoba and Alberta went to a great deal of effort and expense to challenge the shortfall claimed by the railways out of the Crowsnest pass rate agreement. I do not know exactly how much it cost these two provinces, but I know that it cost them many thousands of dollars because it involved a study which went on for well over a year.
In this study in depth, the word of the railway cost accountants was not taken but in many cases a survey was undertaken on the spot to determine the various factors which were included in the cost of grain. I am sure that the minister will recall that the $17 million shortfall claimed by the railways was changed, even in the opinion of the commission, to something around $2 million. When such a claim is made, not only with regard to the Crowsnest pass rates but with any other statutory or fixed rates, that is rates fixed by the commission, who will challenge the railways? The other day I said in the house that
Transportation
to challenge the railways can be a formidable undertaking, and sometimes a very expensive one which involves hiring counsel and cost analysts and, as it is said in the clause-
-persons having knowledge of costing principles or matters that appear to such minister to be relevant to the determination of railway revenues and costs.
It is far too great an undertaking for a municipality, even for a large one.
It was a little too expensive even for the provinces, considering that it is the responsibility of the federal government to defend the public interest in the examination of such costs. And yet, if the provinces of Manitoba and Alberta had not taken on this responsibility on behalf of their farm sector I suppose that it is fair to suggest that the $17 million shortfall claimed by the railways would have been partially if not totally accepted. I suggest that if the figures of the C.P.R. and of the other railways had not been challenged, and a study which had been conducted with a great deal of effort and at a great expense had not been carried out, the railways' contention would have been far stronger.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
That is all I want to say at this time, Mr. Chairman. There are one or two other things I want to talk about under clause 1 of the bill, but I do not think it would be appropriate to raise them now. I have the amendment ready in both English and French, and if the minister would accept it perhaps I could move it, or perhaps I should move it first.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am going to ask the indulgence of the hon. gentleman not to move it at all, but to let me have a copy of it. I have no objection at all to including this provision. Quite the contrary; I would like to have it in clause 74. But I do not think it could very well be related to the amendment moved by the Minister of National Defence. I think it should be in clause 74 generally. The hon. gentleman said he wanted it related, not just to the subject matter of new sections 470 and 471 but to all hearings. This is the way I would like to have it, so we would have a provision that in any hearing of this character this could be done. Certainly, as far as I am concerned I would be very glad to include it. I think it would be an additional safeguard to the treasury and an additional protection to everyone.
As far as I am concerned, I would be very happy to include it in this section. I put it in,

January 26, 1967
Transportation
in the first place, because I thought it was a good idea. If the hon. gentleman would let me have it, I would like a little time to consider it and make a technical assessment of it. I undertake that we will not pass clause 74 before there is an opportunity to deal with it.

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED
speechtext: I agree, Mr. Chairman, and I should like to advise the minister and the members of the committee that there may be a technicality as to where it would best fit into the bill. It does not have to be subsection 4 of new section 470. But I would draw the minister's attention, now that he has the amendment before him, to the fact that the wording is "where in any proceedings before the commission under this act", and so on. It does not say "under this clause" or "under this subclause."

subtopic: SITTING RESUMED
speechtext: I think it might become a new section 472. I do not want it to be related to this specific subject; I want to see the general application of the principle that if at any time there is any reason for this to be done, the representatives of the minister may be there to act on the other side. I think everybody agreed that this was a good idea. But I do not think we want to tie it to this particular amendment.

We have been talking for the most part about transportation over long distances and the abandonment of rail lines. I think we should take a look at the growth of Canada, the increase in its population, and realise that in the year 2,000 it will have a population of between 40 million and 50 million people.
I wish to speak about an area which I know, though the circumstances there are duplicated in many places across the country. I

will take the province of Ontario, a province with a population of six millions which in the year 2,000 will have grown to approximately 12 million people. About one third of the people who live in Canada live today in the province of Ontario. Incidentally, it is interesting to note that about half the people included in that one third live within approximately 100 miles of the city of Toronto. This is a congested area at the present time. In rough figures, a million people go to work, and return, morning and night in Toronto, and in the 100 mile area. The highways which they travel are already overcrowded and the point has been reached at which it is almost impossible technically, and certainly unwise economically, to take more land for through-ways and super highways.
It must also be borne in mind that this is a popular tourist area. This part of Ontario projects so far south in the direction of the United States that the southern part of the province lies south of the northernmost point of the state of California. This means we probably have more American tourists than does any other part of Canada. We cannot cut these people off. Most of them come by car, and we need their dollars to help our balance of payments. So this is the position we are in: We find people going to work, one or two in a car, over highways which are already congested. Thousands of individual cars are travelling into a crowded area when their occupants could be carried more efficiently by train, or other rapid transit. Roughly a million people travel to and from work in this area. One railway line would carry a lot of them into the heart of the city or industrial area, and would eliminate parking problems.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
We are facing a serious problem in air pollution. It takes a motorist in Toronto about an hour to get from downtown to the city limits in the rush hour. He could travel 60 miles in the country in the same length of time, burning approximately the same amount of gas. This is an indication of the amount of pollution and congestion in that area and indicates the need for a rapid transit system.
No railway line in Ontario should be abandoned, and I feel this also applies to many other industrial areas of Canada. In the near future we shall have to rebuild some of the abandoned lines in order to move people to and from work. It is penny wise and pound foolish to abandon railways in a province like
January 26, 1967

Ontario. If certain lines that have been abandoned were in existence today we would be using them to capacity. One line which ran north from Toronto up to Lake Simcoe was abandoned, and had it not been it would remove today a lot of the traffic congestion on the highways.
Slum areas are costing a lot of public money in industrial areas. These sprawling suburban areas are getting completely out of control due to the population explosion. If the trend continues throughout the country, 5 per cent of our population will be living in the rural areas and the other 95 per cent in cities and manufacturing centres. Yet in the great society which we talk about it is estimated that 15 per cent to 20 per cent of the population should live outside the cities.
We shall have to build new towns miles away from cities. I envisage towns like the city of Canberra in Australia, a beautiful city. Those who have visited it know it has no industry. It is the site of the parliament buildings and is a clean, wholesome area in which to live.
I do not believe we have enough railway lines at present in Ontario. We need all that we have, not only to carry freight but to carry people. Commuter trains will be a major factor in transportation, very shortly. Our new towns must be built in locations where land is cheaper, water sources plentiful and air pollution at a minimum. We must start planning for them now, and they must include proper recreational facilities because workers are going to be enjoying more and more leisure time.
The congested areas of the industrial complex of Toronto, which holds roughly 3 million people, needs a rapid transit system. Its problems are duplicated in a minor way in other cities across Canada. Good transportation is necessary so that people can live outside cities in clean, pleasant surroundings in which they can bring up their children. We should be planning now.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have a few remarks to make on this transportation bill. This is the first time since the debate started three weeks ago that I have taken the floor. I did not do so when the various clauses were studied in order to keep my remarks when clause 1 would come up, at which time we could then discuss the bill as a whole.
Mr. Chairman, a while ago I gave figures on the differences in the rates used in the Toronto area and in the city of Montreal. I should like to add a few more, which rates will illustrate somewhat the point I wish to discuss.
For instance, I have here the rates which apply to the transport of wheat, oats, grain and grain products shipped from various parts of the country to Montreal, Halifax, Saint John and Newfoundland. From Fort William and Port Arthur in Ontario to Halifax, a distance of 1694 miles, the rate is 54 cents per hundredweight, from the same points to Saint John, 1463 miles, 54 cents and to other points in Newfoundland; by ship from Halifax or Saint John, 54 cents per hundredweight. In other words, the rate is the same as that which applies to shipments being sent to Halifax.
On the other hand, when shipments are made from Fort William or Port Arthur, to Montreal, a distance of 995 miles, the rate increases to 66 cents per hundredweight. So there is a difference in the rates.
When it starts, for instance, from Sarnia, Toronto, Midland, Walkerville for shipment to Halifax, a distance of 1150 miles, the rate is 26 cents per hundredweight. From the same points to Saint John, New Brunswick, a distance of 1274 miles, the rate is 25 cents per hundredweight, the same as for Newfoundland.
However, if you ship something from Sarnia, Toronto, Walkerville to Montreal, a distance of only 530 miles, then the cost is almost twice as much, namely 48 cents per hundredweight.
Mr. Chairman, we do not object to that. I see no objection to there being such gaps or to subsidies being made to allow those products to reach the maritimes for one must not forget that the maritime provinces are poorer and that they need assistance. We are prepared to accept that, but I quoted these cases
January 26, 1967

Transportation
in order to give another example of discrimination which we are not prepared to accept.
When the government uses the taxes of all the citizens of the country to enable residents of Halifax, of Newfoundland, of New Brunswick or of any maritime province, to pay only half of what the citizens of Montreal or Quebec pay for transport, we are ready to accept that state of affairs, because we consider that the maritimes need help.
It is clear from the figures just quoted by me that the cost is lower in the maritimes for any delivery from points in western Canada or Ontario than what it costs us in Montreal or Quebec.
But it is wrong, inconsistent, irrational and unfair discrimination when after December 12 of every year, ship captains are told, as happened this year in the case of Russian ships reaching the port of Montreal: You have no right to load grain in Montreal. This was reported to me by Canadian and foreign ship captains whom I met in the past week. They are told: You have no right to load grain or wheat in Montreal. If you wish to return to Europe with grain or wheat, get to the port of Halifax in ballast where you can load grain before returning to Europe.
While the Canadian government is paying for the transportation of wheat by railroad from Montreal to Halifax, the ships reach Halifax empty to take in freight there.
But that is not all: the same ship captains will tell you: What stupid things happen in Canada. While the grain elevators are full in Montreal, we are told to reach Halifax in ballast and take in freight there. At present, the average waiting period for ships is six days. The ships reach Halifax empty, while there is still wheat and grain in Montreal. They are empty when they leave Montreal for Halifax. Then they stay there idle for six days, waiting for the grain to reach Halifax from Montreal. And since the shipments are slow in getting to Halifax, the ships have to wait.
Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Transport will agree that it is irrational, illogical. If ships are ready for loading in Halifax, the grain should get there in time. If others are without freight in Montreal, they should be allowed to load there instead of wasting time and money to get to Halifax and wait there before crossing over to Europe. This is a ridiculous system.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
Mr. Chairman, I would also like to hear what the hon. Minister of Transport has to say on some more figures I am going to quote.
Subsidies are granted for all sorts of commodities. For instance, commercial lumber, timber, boards, studs, plywood, etc., are moved in full carloads from British Columbia to Montreal-an average of 2900 miles-at $1.43 per hundredweight whereas full carloads of our Quebec lumber make the Abitibi-Montreal trip-an average of 500 miles

at 43 cents per hundredweight which is twice the cost of bringing western lumber in to Montreal.
Why does it cost twice as much to move lumber from Abitibi to Montreal as it does from British Columbia?
Here sitting next to me is the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Allard) who is aware of the fact that in the eastern townships, Princeville, Beauce, Plessisville, etc., where maple sugar is one of the main resources, this product is shipped at a cost of $1.10 per hundredweight every 340 miles. Why this double standard? Why these special rates?
Mr. Chairman, these rates and subsidies are presently determined by certain individuals who are in a position to make arbitrary decisions in favour of certain parts of the country at the expense of other areas.
These regulations, these rates are published only in English, as the minister knows. The special rates and the subsidies are not published in French but only in English. I have copies of them here, identified by codes known to those who want to use them: CR 200, CF67, CG 130, CG 180, CG 223, E 140 and CRA 6, those are codes to recognize the special rates benefiting all other areas of Canada but not Quebec. In Quebec, we pay full price.
Well, Mr. Chairman, due to such rate differential, the transport of merchandise from British Columbia to Montreal weighing the same as merchandise from Abitibi for delivery in Montreal would cost less. Our maple sugar, a source of wealth for the Eastern townships, does not benefit from any subsidies. Elsewhere, though, subsidies are granted.
Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) should answer this: Why are ships forbidden to load a cargo of wheat or grain in the port of Montreal? Why must they go to Halifax empty and wait there five or six days before loading wheat because none is available?
Can the Minister of Transport reply to this? The ship captains themselves gave me the information.

January 26, 1967
Transportation
And to speak of bilingualism to the Minister of Transport: When ships sail into the gulf they are forced to communicate by radio with the first station on the way into the country, the one situated at Cap-aux-Meules, in the Magdalen Islands. Well, not a word of French is to be had on this radio station. And the same goes for most other radio stations along the St. Lawrence seaway.
The minister should also inquire about that.
Now, Mr. Chairman, there is another point. I know my friend, the hon. member for Sherbrooke also wishes to mention it. The hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier) has referred to it today. Someone is trying to have us pass this bill in haste. In Quebec, the premier objects to that. He is ready to table the letters, but he is waiting for the federal government's permission.
Well, we know implicitly that the premier of Quebec is ready to table the letters. The premier replied as follows to a question from the leader of the opposition in the Quebec legislature: We are ready to table the documents but we are waiting for an answer from the Prime Minister in Ottawa.
Therefore, we want that correspondence. I think the minister is ready to table the correspondence, but I believe he should do so before the passing of this bill, so that we may all be able to know about these objections- and to see whether they are vaild or not.
That problem must be settled before we come to the third reading stage, even before the passing of clause 1 of the bill. I hope the minister will rush the necessary information. I hope he will have relevant remarks to make and that he will give us his opinion in this regard.
The members from Montreal and other areas in the province of Quebec are saying that we imagine we are the only ones to speak on their behalf. In this connection, I will say this: The leader of the opposition in Quebec, who is a member of the Liberal party, and the premier of the province, are of one mind in protesting against the intrusion on the part of the federal government upon a field of provincial jurisdiction. Mr. Chairman, I will not labour the point, merely in order to give them an opportunity to express their view. I am going to give them an opportunity to be the first ones to speak about it, so that they will not be able to accuse me of taking their place. If I have done so on some other occasions, it was because they were not doing it. But now, I am going to let them express

their opinion. They will not be able to make the same accusation in this connection.
Mr. Chairman, I meant to call the attention of the Minister of Transport on one point and I want to give my colleagues in the Liberal party an opportunity to point out something else to him. Once they have dealt with that, I will express my opinion concerning the intrusion of the federal government upon a field of provincial jurisdiction.

Mr. Chairman, I would be quite remiss if before the passing of the bill I did not express, as chairman of the standing committee on transport and communications, my appreciation to members of the committee. As was stated in the report which was filed by the committee, this committee, in hearing the briefs of all the witnesses and considering all the amendments which were presented, held some 33 meetings, heard evidence from some 73 witnesses and received and considered 36 briefs from corporations and individuals who are interested in Bill C-231. In total, since the commencement of this session the committee has held some 72 meetings on all aspects of transportation and communications. I believe that perhaps this is the greatest number of meetings held by any committee in the history of any parliament of Canada.
I as chairman of that committee wish to express my appreciation to all the members of the committee for their diligence in attending the meetings, many of which the press apparently did not consider interesting or newsworthy, although in fact this committee dealt with what is perhaps tlie most important piece of legislation with which this country will have to deal for a good many years.
The committee has given an example of what can be done by members of parliament serving on standing committees of the house.
I do not wish to single out any particular members, but again I feel I would be remiss in my duty if I did not express particular appreciation to three members of that committee who attended its meetings every day and who were very diligent in their work. I am referring to the hon. members for Moose Mountain, Moose Jaw-Lake Centre and Kindersley. I think that these three members should be singled out for their efforts. I am not trying to take away from the work of the other members from all parties in the house,
January 26, 1967

but I do feel that all members of the committee will understand why I have singled out these three members of the committee.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
I think all members of the committee were deeply appreciative of the attendance of the Minister of Transport at our meetings. It helped us expedite consideration of the briefs and the passage of the bill through committee. When the minister was not able to attend a committee meeting, the Minister without Portfolio, the hon. member for St. Law-rence-St. George, was there. This was of great assistance to the standing committee and perhaps should be an example followed by other ministers.
I would be remiss if I did not convey the thanks of the committee to the deputy minister of transport and the officials who were present at our meetings. The deputy minister and his officials were of great help to the minister. They were available at every meeting to assist hon. members with regard to questions that they asked, and in preparing amendments and summaries of briefs for the assistance of members of the committee. They helped in preparing in a very informative and summary manner amendments that were considered in relation to Bill C-231, which was of great assistance to the members of the committee in their work. On behalf of all members of the committee I want to thank the deputy minister and the officials of the Department of Transport for the work they did in assisting us in our consideration of this bill.
Members from all sides of the house were co-operative in considering a bill of vital importance to the national interest, a bill that had been talked about for many years and which was the subject of at least two royal commissions, the Turgeon commission and the MacPherson commission. Our meetings showed that the members were knowledgeable in this subject, had done their homework and had read and considered all the briefs presented to the committee. They also showed they were knowledgeable in the questioning of the witnesses who appeared before the committee. They showed that they knew what they were talking about. I would suggest that on many occasions the witnesses were somewhat surprised at the questions asked by the members of the committee, and were at times taken aback in answering some of them, because I believe the committee members showed that sometimes they knew more than the witness about the subject in question.
Transportation
All the briefs were carefully considered. I want to thank the Minister of Transport and the government in this respect, because it showed that the department and the minister were not inflexible in receiving suggestions from those who presented briefs. I think all members will agree with me that a great many amendments put forward in committee were made as a result of briefs presented by individuals, provincial governments and companies that appeared before the committee. I believe this helped many of us in our consideration of the bill and showed us the importance of inflexibility in regard to a bill that was in the national interest, and would mean that once and for all Canada would have a national transportation policy.
I also believe our experience in the committee showed up some of the weaknesses of the standing committee structure. Our committee retained an eminent economist, Dr. Armstrong, who had worked on the MacPherson royal commission. Perhaps other committees, and especially those dealing with important legislation, should be allowed to obtain the expertise of counsel and economists in order to deal more effectively with these matters. I would also like to thank the vice-chairman of the committee who, when the chairman was not able to attend on a few occasions, took his place at the meetings. I think we now have a very good base from which to move forward as far as a transportation policy is concerned. I will not take up the time of the committee to deal with the different aspects of transportation. Many hon. members of this house have done so already. I just want again to express my deep appreciation to all members of the committee for the courtesy they showed me and for the very kind words many of them had for me.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to thank the members of the committee for this opportunity to avail myself of a few moments of the committee's time in the discussion on clause 1 of Bill No. C-231, an act to define and implement a national transportation policy for Canada. The hon. member for Hamilton West has put the committee in a very good mood and has named so many of the hard working members of the standing committee. I wish to thank him personally for his kind reference to myself, the hon. member for Moose Jaw, the hon. member for Kindersley and other hon. members whom he mentioned. But in making this passing reference we should not overlook the chairman of the committee, the hon. member for Hamilton West himself.
As the hon. member pointed out, this bill was one of the most important, most contentious and contained some of the biggest problems, I think, of any bill ever presented to a committee of the house. His guidance and perseverance, together with the assistance of the vice-chairman, I believe went a long way in facilitating the progress we had already made in passing the bill.
The hon. member overlooked other very capable members besides members of his own party, who also made contributions to the work of the committee. I think I should single out for particular mention the hon. member for Acadia. I feel that he is a man who has spent more time on and done more research into the problems of transportation, and has made, I believe, a greater contribution toward the passage of this bill, than any other individual in the house.
In saying that, we should not forget the chairman of our group, the hon. member for Saint John-Albert, the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, the hon. member for Pictou, the hon. member for Wellington-Huron and, of course, the minister himself. It was appreciated by the members of the committee that, although he had problems in dealing with much of the testimony presented to the committee, the minister was on the job day after day doing everything he could to assist us in carrying out a proper study toward the development of this bill. It was

because of the co-operation of the minister that many contentious points were made capable of solution, and it was helpful when he agreed to accept amendments made by the members. In this way we were able to make the progress we did.
Having said that, Mr. Chairman, there is the usual "but". Personally I feel, as a member from western Canada, that this is not yet a good bill. After all, we have been working on a piecemeal basis on transportation legislation since back in 1898. We have been bringing forward and developing certain modes of transportation and have developed, as I say, a sort of piecemeal type of program in Canada. Naturally, it is very difficult to take one encompassing piece of legislation such as Bill No. C-231 and expect it to bring us up to date completely, and be a perfect product in the end result. I think evidence of this fact is what transpired during the course of our committee study. In the committee something like 50 or 60 amendments were put forward by witnesses. We had to contend with those. The fact that there were so many amendments is evidence that it was not a good bill to start with.
I have not been able to keep track of the number of amendments placed before this committee of the whole. They have all been important; they have all been well debated. There is an indication that many more amendments may be introduced before this bill comes finally to the point of what I think is necessary in order to achieve a modern system of transportation in Canada.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
I am disturbed about the complete transfer of principle or concept from the old transport board to the new commission, so far as rate setting is concerned. It would appear as though the minister was rather cosy with the railroads in drafting this legislation. I have heard remarks to this effect. In fact, I am just wondering whether the minister, instead of aspiring to the Senate some time in the future, may be thinking of becoming president of the Canadian National.
In other words, Mr. Chairman, I do not believe all modes of transport have received adequate debate or consideration in this bill. I am thinking of transport by air. Here is a developing mode of transport that has grown up, almost like Topsy, in recent years. I believe the competitive principle should be applied to this mode of transport rather than to rail rates.
January 2S, 1967



There is also the St. Lawrence seaway in connection with which problems are developing. Yesterday the hon. member tor Acadia mentioned the problem of seaway tolls. The people of western Canada, as captive shippers, are very dependent upon the seaway and shippers through the great lakes, I do not believe this aspect has been fully covered in our discussion.
The section of the bill dealing with pipe lines is another important aspect. This important mode of transport, although covered in the bill, is still subject to many limitations. The hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare brought to the attention of hon. members the inadequacies in this legislation in so far as pipe lines are concerned. As members of the committee know, this man has spent a lifetime in the oil industry and knows something about the transportation of this particular commodity. In fact I believe he mentioned he had a chance to look at something like 15 or 16 bills related to pipe line transport in other countries.
One of my colleagues says that this man helped to build 15 or 16 pipe lines. If we had had the time, here was an opportunity to explore the knowledge he had, and possibly have developed a better bill thereby. When we did criticize various aspects of the bill, I do not believe it was necessary for the minister to hide behind the fact the Conservative party had set up the MacPherson royal commission in the first place. I know on various occasions this hint was thrown out by the minister, that after all the Conservatives set up a commission which made certain recommendations, and therefore they must be good. This does not necessarily follow, Mr. Chairman. The government does not have to adopt any of the recommendations if they do not desire to do so. Many of these recommendations were worthy of consideration and we did consider them. When I say I am not satisfied with the bill, I think it is a wrong concept to take the lid off and allow the railways to set rates as high as the traffic will bear. This is what we have done in this piece of legislation.
I was naturally happy to see section 329 of clause 50 voted down by the committee. This directly preserved the farmer's Magna Carta of 1897 on rates affecting the movement of grain or the Crowsnest pass rates as they are called. Had the minister's amendment to clause 94 been allowed it would have been, as the hon. Leader of the Opposition said yesterday, like putting a weasel in a chicken coop, or the first chink in the armour, or hole in the 23033-779
Transportation
dike. The supposition now that the Crowsnest pass rates cost the railways $2 million is inaccurate in this day and age. This estimate is based on cost accounting practices that were questionable in the first place, and in the second place, the figures were based on traffic back in 1950 to 1960.
Members of the committee and people at large in this country, particularly those in western Canada, realize the vast changes in economic growth since 1960. These changes have been reflected in the movement of grain. This year we have produced something like 800 million bushels of grain in the three prairie provinces. If we include flax, oats, barley and corn, the total volume would reach something like 1,200 million bushels. Then, the discovery of vast deposits of potash in Saskatchewan since the time of the MacPherson royal commission has greatly enhanced the economy of the railways. I believe therefore we have been basing some of this legislation on figures which were outdated.
I do not believe the change in concept to allow rates in Canada to be set by competition will work well in a country of such vast geographic proportions. If we compare Canada to the United States, we find we have a somewhat greater geographic area. The United States has a population of something like 200 million people. So as a result you would feel that this concept of setting rates by competition would work much better there. As the members of the committee and the minister know, from the testimony we heard, the United States set rates in all fields of transportation by regulation. This principle applies also to other countries of the commonwealth. Here we have a young country with one of the greatest geographic areas in the world, sparsely populated, trying to use a concept which I do not believe will work too effectively.
We should have listened to the evidence given by Professors Borts and Williams, to which reference has been made by other members of the committee. I feel these were the two top expert witnesses who were brought in on behalf of the Government of Manitoba to testify from their knowledge and experience in transportation as to what they would suggest could be done to improve this bill. Of course their suggestion was that we completely reverse the concept and regulate rates.
Now, having said that, Mr. Chairman, I should like to conclude my remarks by making one or two short references to rail line

January 26, 1967
Transportation
abandonment. I have often spoken in the house on this subject. As I pointed out on several occasions, I had a sad experience in representing an area which had a rail line abandonment of the greatest magnitude of any place in western Canada, some 122 miles. When this application was before the Board of Transport Commissioners, I did a lot of research into the problem and know something about the sociological and economic disruptions created by rail line abandonment.
I do not want to pursue the subject any further than to say I am a little concerned about the principle that has been adopted temporarily by the government under the guidance of the Minister of Transport. I refer to the freeze on rail line abandonments until 1975. It seems to me that 1975 is now too far away. I am afraid we are going to be opening another kettle of fish at that time. I believe there should have been more effort to bring the rationalization principle into effect, so there would be no necessity for opening this subject again. In the meantime we are going to be faced with a series of applications for the abandonment of short lines which will come before the new commission which is set up.
I am disappointed that the minister did not see fit to include in this legislation a principle which I have advocated on numerous occasions. I refer to the fact that if a line is to be abandoned after proper study, there should be a freeze on the abandonment order for five years. This would give businesses, farmers and municipalities adjacent to that line a chance to liquidate their businesses, provide roads to replace the railroads, give the farmers a chance to remove their permit books to other areas and so make the necessary readjustments when the line has been taken out. However, we may still have a chance to see that principle incorporated at a later date.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
We have done our best to produce a good bill. I am not trying to discredit anybody in saying this because I think we have done our best. However, I still feel that the bill falls far short of what is necessary to provide a good transportation policy. For example we should have incorporated in the bill a clause to the effect that the government in five or six years time should review the legislation and iron out any anomalies or bugs which might have become apparent by then. Had this been done, Mr. Chairman, even though criticism has been directed toward the bill we would have left ourselves .in the position where the

people of Canada would be able to say that the government had co-operated with the opposition to come up with the best possible bill, and I think the people would be well satisfied. We have a right to be a little critical of the bill, and in concluding my remarks I express the hope that the legislation works out better than I think it will at the present time.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY

speechtext:
The house resumed consideration in committee of Bill No. C-231, to define and implement a national transportation policy for Canada, to amend the Railway Act and other acts in consequence thereof, and to enact other consequential provisions-Mr. Pickers-gill-Mr. Batten in the chair.
On clause 1-National transportation policy.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR DEFINITION AND IMPLEMENTATION OF NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few concluding remards on clause 1 before we pass committee stage of this large and complex bill. I should like to endorse the remarks made by the chairman of the committee on transportation and communications, the hon. member for Hamilton West, with regard to the expressions of appreciation of the minister and deputy minister, the officials of the department and a number of members of the committee. The meetings were far longer, and the committee dealt with a far more complex matter than any standing committee of this house has had for a long time. This does not take anything away from the excellent work other committees are doing at this time, but I am convinced that this bill of more complex nature than any other being considered at this time.
Having said that, Mr. Chairman, and without any reservations as to those expressions of appreciation, I would also raise a word of caution regarding the application of this bill and its effects. I know the minister is aware that when this bill is in full force and effect there will be a very significant increase in freight rates. There will also be a very significant increase in the amount of revenue obtained by the railways from those freight rates. I say that because in many areas there will have to be a substitution of higher revenue from freight rates for the subsidies which have been paid by the federal government, which in the current fiscal year amount to about $110 million.
I agree that this will be done gradually, but in addition to subsituting for these subsidies 23033-7791
Transportation
revenue from freight rates equivalent to those now being paid, there is also a rather significant increase in cost to the railways which will have to be met out of the same revenue derived from freight rates.
For example, we all know that in August and September, 1966 this parliament ordered the railway workers back to work, and at the same time guaranteed to them not less than an 18 per cent increase in wages spread over three years. We also know that mediation has been going on as a result of this order of parliament and one recommendation has been that the increase which is to be spread over this three-year period should be as much as 24 per cent.
I am not suggesting that any of these railway workers are receiving too much compared with wages paid for comparable jobs in other industries, but I do say we have to face the fact that an enormous increase in revenue will be required to be raised from freight rates not only to compensate for the loss of subsidies but also to meet increasing costs.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
I hope that the commission will be ever diligent as it applies these new provisions, to make sure that each rate and each category of freight will bear a fair share of increases. In the past it appears to have been too easy for the railways to apply the increases to those categories and shippers captive to the railways. There has not been a comparable increase in rates in areas where there has been effective competition from motor transport, air freight carriers or shipment by water.
Though we introduce a new concept, that railways shall be competitive and find almost all their revenues from competing in the marketplace, as a substitute for subsidies, we must remember that the captive shipper still needs the protection of political action by the parliament of Canada.
Throughout the debate on the bill members from various areas of this country have said they were not quite satisfied with the terminology, with the wording in various clauses. They have asked the minister from time to time what certain things mean; if there appeared to be ambiguity or misunderstanding in language, they asked how that could be applied to transportation. The minister has given assurances of what is intended. Time after time we accepted from the minister his assurances of what parts of the bill are intended to do, and we accepted those assurances despite the interpretation which may be

January 26, 1967
Transportation
given to some clauses by others. I admonish the minister again, if I may, to live up to these assurances, that this act may be an improvement in the transportation of Canada rather than a detriment to certain areas, regions, industries or economic sectors.
In conclusion I wish to say to the minister, to the chairman of the committee, and to all members of that committee that we hope the fruits of our labours, if I may call it that -because this labour has been going on for a long time-will in fact mean an improvement and benefit for Canada. We hope we shall gain knowledge from our experience of applying this bill in the first few months, so that when we come back in the next session, or the session after that based on the experience we have gained we may make the amendments necessary to make transportation a real asset to Canada from one end to the other.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I realize that in the circumstances the minister is most anxious to conclude the study of his bill after all he has had to go through in this house in the last three weeks but, to make him feel better, I can assure him that my remarks will be brief.
I noticed a little earlier that the time had come for congratulations; on both sides words of appreciation were said about this one and that one. I think that something would be missing if someone did not rise at a given moment to stress, to underline the infinite patience shown by the minister during the debate. Sometimes we had the impression-we who followed the debate as objectively as possible-that he was drowning the opposition under a wave of politeness, so eager was he to listen to suggestions and even to ask for them.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I will be happy with a few short remarks to say that, in my opinion, the debate was quite instructive, from my own standpoint. Personally, I learned a lot about the economic activities of that area called the Crowsnest pass and the Pacific coast. I heard more about the Crowsnest pass in the last three weeks that in my whole life before; that name which to me was only a rather abstract geographic point takes on today a meaning full of possibilities for the future of our country. I wish therefore to thank my colleagues for what they taught me.
In my few remaining remarks, perhaps I might reply to some statements made by my

colleague the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire). Of course, I am not expected to agree with him always. I would not like hon. members to think that I hate him; on the contrary, I am among those who do not wish the sinner to die, but to repent and be saved.
Therefore, knowing that the hon. member for Lapointe is intelligent and that he has an impressive gift of speech and unusually quick reactions, I believe we should charitably seize every opportunity to try to keep him in the right path because, talented as he is, he could be of service to the country instead of trying to harm it as he has been doing for some time. It is in this spirit, Mr. Chairman, that I would like to draw attention to some of the things he said.
Tonight he said things which impressed me and which would have, normally, done so. Besides, when I listen to the hon. member for Lapointe, I must say that I am very attentive because, occasionally, he says sensible things. He enjoys periods of lucidity, but not necessarily when he chooses to describe the members who represent Montreal, as he did recently. Then, he reminds me of the man who went to see an optician and asked him: "Can you make me a pair of glasses so that I can read"? The optician took pains and made him something a little special but the man came back a week later and said: "But I cannot read with your glasses". After a rather long study of the situation, the optician found out that the man could not read.
There are things that the hon. member for Lapointe cannot read, because he looks at them in a light which is different from everybody else's. However, as we wish him no harm, instead of following the advice of the evil spirits who suggested to ignore him, I think that, charitably, we should apply ourselves to bringing him back on the right track.
Mr. Chairman, some members who are listening to me are anxious to see how I will conclude. I was surprised a moment ago to see the member for Lapointe shaking the minister violently, hoping that tomorrow's newspapers will mention the fact that the member for Lapointe reminded the Minister of Transport that he was committing a heresy by encroaching upon a field where constitutionally the federal government should not interfere. He evidently missed the definite answer given by the minister around 5.45 this afternoon. 1 was impressed to see how categorical the minister was. He was expressing the viewpoint of the Prime Minister (Mr. January 26, 1967

Pearson); he said so himself. But on that matter, my opinion is not very unlike that of the member for Lapointe. I simply blame him once again for not being often enough in the house.
However, I will say to the minister that there is obviously confusion in the minds, since we see that even lawyers, who should be experts in legal and constitutional matters, are not agreeing on that; in fact, lawyers of all political affiliations are upholding divergent opinions concerning the constitutionality or unconstitutionality of an act. For instance, the leader of the opposition and the head of the government in Quebec are two lawyers who maintain that this is not constitutional while in the federal government, lawyers are advising the minister to say that it is constitutional. But we have to come to a conclusion for the guidance of the public in search of the truth.
I would like to suggest to the minister to develop the comments he made in the house and the answer he gave and prepare in his usual masterful fashion which we admire, a press release where he could line up all the arguments proving that he is right, and let them be known throughout Canada. This would put an end to ambiguity and misunderstanding, and prevent certain circles from brandishing scarecrows, to frighten the people who eventually imagine that Ottawa is a bogyman who tries continually, year after year, to infringe provincial rights.
When this is true, it should be blamed; when not, persons who are solicitous of the truth should not do so.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
Therefore, I repeat that the minister should clarify the situation in an unqualified statement spread across the country, so that people may know whether or not it is constitutional.
Like those who are constructively trying to find more practical solutions, it seemed to me that the minister was right when he said that we were legislating on interprovincial and international transport; that field comes under federal jurisdiction. That strikes me as being true, because I went through the bill once more to find if it were in any way dealing with provincial transport and I could not find anything of the sort, except, of course, that provincial transport companies wishing to go from one province to another or to the United States will have to comply with this legislation. I think this matter warrants
Transportation
the federal government's intervention, because the existing mess had to be tidied up, what with different legislation and procedures from one province to another.
Personally, I was impressed by the minister's answer, but some Canadians may not have read it or may not have had the opportunity to consider it; he should make his opinion widely known, complete it, support it with arguments, and even send a French copy to the hon. member for Lapointe as well as to the leader of the opposition and the Quebec premier who seem to be people of good will.
The hon. member for Lapointe-no, I am not judging anybody, I leave that up to Providence-mentioned things which nevertheless seemed justified. He said, for instance, that the first short-wave station with which ships entering the St. Lawrence can communicate answers in English only; well, it is inconceivable that this should happen in the province of Quebec.
And that reminds me; we have this problem in our control towers at Montreal. Not at Quebec city, however, where both English and French are spoken. I am speaking of incoming planes. Unfortunately, most of the answers are given in English at Montreal. I speak from personal experience. I travel by plane once in a while. However, I feel bilingual personnel is essential. I agree with the hon. member for Lapointe here, because there you have pilots of all nationalities, speaking various languages.
I was also impressed when he quoted figures emphasizing rate differentials from one city to another. This should prove to the hon. member for Lapointe that I am no fanatic; I am giving him the credit he deserves.
I will not deny what I cannot prove, but I did check on one of his statements. A few days ago, the hon. member for Lapointe had told me: "Russian ships come into Montreal, unload their cargo and are not allowed to take on a load of grain for the return trip. They are told to head for Halifax, where they have to wait a few days". I told him at the time: "This does not seem logical. If it is true, then something must be done."
I went to see those who know what they are talking about. We have grain elevators too, you know. We also have people in the grain business. There are some in Montreal too. Well, I got my information from these people. I was given what I feel is a plausible explanation, which I am giving to the house. Hon. members may check on it if they so desire.

January 26, 1967
Transportation
I was told that the grain coming from western Canada and from the great lakes area, comes to Montreal, Trois-Rivieres and Quebec city mostly by ship during the navigation season. A very small percentage of the grain production is shipped by rail, it seems.
Early in winter, before the season closes, elevators are filled in Montreal, Trois-Rivieres and Quebec city in order to serve consumers in those three areas.
Therefore, from the economic point of view, it would not be wise to let Russian or other foreign ships take aboard our winter supplies which would force us to bring in our own supplies by rail, which would cost more. Another possibility would be to have our livestock tighten their belts. Therefore, this regulation was made, so that foreign ships would not come and get our winter supplies. We need them for ourselves and our silos; our elevators are not large enough to provide for local consumption as well as for exports. Therefore they are being told; Go get some in Halifax. In Halifax, shipping goes on the year round. It seems the elevators there are larger, local consumption is not as heavy and that it is less expensive to send the Lakers over there to get unloaded directly rather than to send them to Montreal and Trois-Rivieres and have them take freight there and be sent to the Atlantic coast.
That was the explanation I got and I think it plausible. Another reason I have to find it plausible is that in checking and doublechecking I got the same answer.
And this proves that we can easily hear about things, in this house, that seem to us fantastic and astounding and that may create a scandal the following day in the newspapers. I am wondering whether in the long run, by dint of crying wolf, we are not thus creating a feeling of mistrust among the people. We could normally influence the public if we were careful to cry wolf only when the wolf is really at the door and to cry fire when the fire is really burning.
Again, I am not in a position to question the other assertions made by the hon. member for Lapointe. If the figures he mentioned are correct, well, I am saying to the minister it is about time to take care of that situation and to remedy that injustice, should it exist.
But once again, I would like us to have an opportunity to check the statements of the hon. member for Lapointe before blaming anybody. If he is right, the situation should be coped with.

On the other hand, if an irresponsible accusation comes out of the blue, as in the case of the ship captains who are being required to go to Halifax with empty ships, I say that the bad impression created among the people should be corrected.
Mr. Chairman, I believe this house does not ever bring forth perfect bills. The one which we have considered was a difficult one and the debate was protracted.
I feel this discussion has been constructive on the whole and I believe it is valuable piece of legislation, though imperfect. There will certainly be some people who will complain about it, after some experience. But, I presume that parliament will have the privilege of reviewing this legislation every year in order to improve it and amend it so that it will meet the needs of all Canadians.
There are two other things I would like to point out, Mr. Chairman. They have already been mentioned, but I believe they will never be emphasized enough. First, there is the matter of railway and steamship companies that do not pay taxes to municipalities, as everyone does, and of the grants which the federal government must pay in lieu of the taxes those companies should pay. But it is alleged that the Queen must not normally be taxed; that is going a bit too far because I cannot see what the C.N.R. has to do with the Queen, but let us say it is acceptable. Nonetheless, I would say that the subsidies paid by the federal government to the municipalities are, in most cases, inadequate and determined unilaterally.
I suggest that consultations should be held with bodies representing municipalities, such as the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities which has a very active and very capable committee, since the chairman of its harbours committee has recently been appointed member of the National Harbours Board. I refer to the former mayor of Halifax and a former member of this house, Mr. John Lloyd. The federation has a harbours committee which is actively engaged in all matters concerning towns where there is a port and I think the government should get in touch with this committee to determine the fair and reasonable amounts that municipalities should receive in subsidies. I say that in most cases, they are insufficient and do not cover the services rendered by the municipalities to the national harbours.
January 26, 1967



[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
Another thing I mentioned briefly in my last remarks and which I should like to emphasize because it is probably more important than it would seem on first sight-and I know that all members of this house who have sat on city councils will support what I am suggesting. I claim that it is unfair to require municipalities to pay a share of the cost of tunnels or overpasses that are required to eliminate level crossings. I think the cost of those things should be paid for by the federal government and by the company concerned.
I say the municipalities cannot afford to meet those costs, those capital expenditures and that it is unfair to force them to do it. I mention this to the minister so that instructions may be given to the transport commission whose responsibilities, I assume, will include making such recommendations.
No one will deny that Canadian municipalities are in an alarming financial situation; they lack the resources of the provincal and federal governments to fulfil their responsibilities to their residents. Tax sharing arrangements are being delayed for all sorts of reasons, good or bad, while the municipalities are faced with most difficult problems. Those should not be increased by requiring them to pay sums in excess of their means because, in their own jurisdiction, city councillors are often blamed by the voters, the citizens, for failing to eliminate fast enough level crossings within their territory.
Mr. Chairman, I conclude by repeating another thing, and through repetition, its importance perhaps will finally sink in. Several of my colleagues have said that in this day and age, transportation is extremely important for the country's economy and that in the years to come, we shall have to provide especially for an extensive development of air transport. I say to the minister that a special effort should be made in order to fully anticipate the needs of private aviation if it is to develop normally.
When I speak of private aviation, I do not mean mere amateurs who fly for an hour or two around the town where they live on Sunday morning, but of a sector which is developing very rapidly, that is, private airlines which operate their own planes and American companies which come to Canada with their own planes. I think an overall plan should be designed, particularly with regard to the construction of a greater number of primary, secondary and tertiary landing strips to
Transportation
encourage development in this sector of the industry.
There are other sectors which I shall not deal with so as not to prolong the debate. I should like the minister to remember the essential part of my recommendation, which is that a subcommittee of this Canadian Transport Commission, perhaps, could be instructed to make a complete study of the needs of private aviation in Canada, in view of the developments which we may expect within the next 10 or 15 years.
Mr. Chairman, to show that I am objective and do not suffer from a chronic allergy, I invite the hon. Minister of Transport to inquire into the accusations made by the hon. member for Lapointe who said that there are tariff differences. I suggest that the minister take steps to remedy the situation, because these differences will produce cases of injustice which can easily be exploited by those who want to make capital out of national disunity.

Mr. Chairman, when some of the clauses dealing with air transportation were being discussed it was suggested that anyone wishing to speak on that topic should wait until clause 1 was called again for discussion. Before proceeding further, on behalf of our party I would like to express our appreciation to the hon. member for Medicine Hat for his contribution to the deliberation of the standing committee, and in this debate. He was our main spokesman throughout the debate and we appreciate the effort he made.
The first few words of clause 1 read:
It is hereby declared that an economic and efficient transportation system making the best use of all available modes of transportation at the lowest total cost is essential.
I am sure I am not the only Canadian who is a bit concerned about the possibility of this ever being more than a pious hope and wishful thinking. I read a week or two ago that Air Canada had committed itself to the purchase of supersonic aircraft. It has plans to purchase four of the Anglo French Concorde and six of the American supersonic aircraft that are now in the planning stage. I expect there are a variety of reasons why Air Canada is going ahead with these plans, but I would like to draw the attention of the committee and of the new Transport Commission to an article which appeared in Harper's Magazine in July, 1966, entitled "The Case against the Supersonic Transport" by John E. Gibson.

January 26, 1967
Transportation
In it Mr. Gibson refers to the problems that have arisen in North American transport as a result of over-enthusiasm for the railroad when it was a new method of transport, and when it was revolutionary. I am sure that many of the hours of debate we have had in this session on transport resulted because of mistakes that were made when the railway was a new, experimental, untried form of transportation, and that we are paying now for over-optimism at that time. Yet we seem about to repeat the cycle when it comes to supersonic aircraft.
The article that I have mentioned lists some of the technical difficulties that are involved in this new form of aircraft. They are truly formidable. In speaking of the Concorde the writer says that in essence it will be obsolete before it leaves the drafting table. He also writes of the possible dangers to passengers. These planes will fly at much greater heights than we are accustomed to, and Mr. Gibson gives this startling warning:
At 70,000 feet, the proposed cruising altitude of the SST, there will be no need of oxygen masks if cabin pressure is lost. The reason is that the human body undergoes explosive decompression, the blood boils, and death occurs within several seconds. This happens whether or not one wears an oxygen mask. The only safeguard is an astronaut type pressure suit.
Designers feel that the safest sort of supersonic aircraft would have no windows, yet the aircraft which Air Canada proposes to purchase will have windows. The article goes on to mention a great many other things, such as the eroding effect of rain at supersonic speeds and so on.
[DOT] (10:30 p.m.)
The real problems, however, are not in that area. Having discussed this, he goes on to say that the real problem of supersonic transport is that it cannot make money. Yet Air Canada, which is a crown corporation, is going into a field in which money cannot be made. This means that we will have to pay for it through taxation on higher prices, but it will be paid for and paid for many times. With the announcement of the proposed purchases we have also had the beginning of a program to condition the public of Canada to the acceptance of this. Already we have been told that a premium rate will be paid for this type of transport. Already we have been told that the operating costs will be 50 per cent higher than they are in respect of the conventional subsonic transport with which we are now familiar.
We might wonder why a crown corporation has gone so far as to commit itself in this

way. To those people who are wondering why, I would recommend to them a series of lectures which have been given in the last two months by the economist John Kenneth Galbraith which have been published in the Listener. These lectures were given over the B.B.C. He talks about modem technology having destroyed the market, and because the market has been destroyed it becomes essential for government or the great corporations to replace the market and in effect, to guarantee a market. This can be done by the advertising industry using its persuasive means to create a market, or it can be done by a government subsidy.
In the case of the supersonic transport it would seem that the government of Canada, through its crown corporation Air Canada, is guaranteeing a market for one of the most expensive experiments ever undertaken. In its development the Concorde already has cost $1,500 million, and it is not yet in the air. I am sure the cost of the American plane will be even higher than that. Although we in Canada no longer have the kind of aircraft industry which could venture into this sort of an experiment, none the less we will be subsidizing these two experiments, one from Europe and the other outside our border in North America.
I would question whether the Canadian public is prepared to subsidize this type of transport to the extent necessary, because not only will the cost of each airplane be involved, which will be in the vicinity of $40 million, and the operating costs, but also of course there is the cost of the drastic alterations, which have to be made in the runways, in the flight patterns, in the safety precautions and in a host of other areas, if this type of transport is to be used at all.
One might wonder about the reason for this. I expect Air Canada and perhaps the government of Canada have realized there no longer is any free market in the aircraft industry; otherwise what would be the reason for agreeing in advance, when neither of them has been flown, to purchase four Concordes and six American planes? Why not wait to see whether they are feasible at all? Here we have a very fine example of a market being guaranteed. No opportunity is being given for anything like a competitive trial between the two planes, nor even a competitive trial between the supersonic and the subsonic.
One would expect that there would be no advantage in gaining an hour or two in a flight across the Atlantic if more and more
January 26, 1967

time is involved in getting to the airport. It seems to me that it is unwise for a nation with a population such as ours and a country as small as ours to become involved in an experiment such as this. When there is a need for development in other areas in our own country, such as education and research, I do not think we should commit so much of our economic effort to bringing our air line into the supersonic category. I know that these days this is one of the methods employed to buy international prestige; but I doubt really whether Canadians are prepared or should be prepared to pay that price for international prestige. I expect, however, that we will do this, because it will be treated as an inevitability. I expect that Air Canada is above and beyond the reach of any transport board which would be set up as a result of this legislation, because aircraft corporations, not only in Canada but in all countries, seem to be able to put themselves well out of the reach of democratic government.
If there is a need to subsidize technology I believe we should see that it is subsidized in areas which would be more truly productive for the benefit of mankind. Perhaps we should use whatever influence we have left in the United Nations in an effort to get together with the nations in a discussion as to the advisability of continuing this race for higher speeds at increasingly diminishing returns forever and ever.
This is all I have to say in respect of transport, Mr. Chairman, but I do feel that unless there is a close and careful examination made of the future of air transport, and the costs and problems involved in the course on which this nation has embarked, clause 1 of Bill C-231 will be wishful thinking indeed.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it seems that this long debate on Bill C-231 is finally coming to an end. We now are on clause 1, and since this is the clause for which I have been waiting, I have a few remarks I should like to make. First of all, I think this debate has proven the value of the committees system. I do not think any bill has ever had a more careful scrutiny. At least this would seem to be the case now, when we are at the end of a long and arduous debate and see the gentlemanly way in which hon. members treat each other. I must say, however, that this whole proposition of putting all of Canada's transport under one omnibus committee leaves some doubt in my mind as to whether any committee could handle this onerous task. I would go further and say that any minister 23033-780
Transportation
charged with the responsibility of overseeing the work of such a committee would have his hands full. Therefore I should like to suggest to the minister, and through him to the government, that they give very careful consideration to dividing the responsibility of the Minister of Transport, if not into two complete ministries at least to the point of establishing the position of an associate minister for air.
[DOT] (10:40 p.m.)
As the last speaker has pointed out today, air is taking a more prominent place than ever before in the economic affairs of Canada and of the whole world.
It seems to me that if we are to keep in pace with the jet age we need the full time of a minister who would answer all those questions with regard to air transport and, in the very near future, space control, as well as questions on the research and development which is required if we are not to have chaos in the air industry. Certainly the minister who is responsible for co-ordinating our railroad, pipe line and water transport will have more than his hands full. It may be that in the future we may not have as capable a minister as we have at present who, when all is said, has given a great deal of energy and thought to these matters. I cannot say that I have always agreed with his conclusions but his energy is certainly beyond argument.
To be specific on two matters, let me remind the house that we have been told by the ministry over and over again that our Crowsnest freight rates will be protected and honoured and that indeed this commission, when it is in full operation, will attack Canada's transportation problems with vision. We must have the courage and vision to see the greater Canada which must emerge, and this will mean connecting the railway lines which have not been linked in the past. We must have the courage to build and anticipate the tonnage which will travel over the new railway lines.
I join other members of the house in saying that, whether or not it is wishful thinking, we hope that the new experiment in co-ordinating Canada's transportation system will bear the fruit that all of us sincerely anticipate.

Mr. Chairman, I shall be brief. I merely wish to deal with some views expressed by the minister this afternoon with regard to a question I put at the start of the sitting.

January 26, 1967
Transportation
First of all, I shall remind the minister that on September 6, in this house, while he was making some remarks on the proposed resolution, I concluded my remarks as follows:
How will the provincial government react to <his resumption, by the federal government, of (ome authority in the field of interprovincial highway traffic?
I put that question to the minister, and I suggested to him, on that and other occasions, that he should consult or get in touch with the Quebec provincial government, which is rightly concerned about certain initiatives of the central government.
I notice that since September 6-I know that the minister is very busy-he probably did not have the opportunity or did not want to take the initiative to contact the Quebec government. And what I was expecting finally burst out.
Today's newspapers report, as pointed out by the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier), that the Quebec legislature, Premier Daniel Johnson and the leader of the opposition, Mr. Jean Lesage, agreed on that matter. The hon. member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Mongrain) looked surprised a little earlier that two lawyers could agree on an important point.
Yes, Mr. Chairman, yesterday in the Quebec legislative assembly, the premier and the leader of the official opposition agreed to protest to the central government about Bill No. C-231 on transportation.
The Minister of Transport answered, towards the end of the afternoon, that he had discussed the matter with the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and that he intended to table tomorrow the correspondence exchanged between the federal government, the central government, and the Quebec government about the matter. The Quebec premier and the Quebec leader of the opposition were not the only ones who protested. In fact, a few weeks ago we read reports in the press according to which the provincial minister of highways, Mr. Lizotte, protested vehemently against certain tendencies revealed in Bill C-231.
This evening, we are asked to sit until the bill reaches third reading. This is absolutely illogical. In conscience, Mr. Chairman, we should be able to read the correspondence to find out on what criteria the Quebec government based its protests and, also, to study the replies given by the federal authorities to the Quebec government with regard to the controversy about Bill C-231.

That is why I would rather we did not vote this evening, we did not agree to third reading, prior to having had the opportunity to-

I wonder if I may interrupt the hon. gentleman. There is no intention whatever to ask the house to accept third reading of the bill tonight. All we are doing is trying to complete the committee stage. In fact I do not think that under the rules we could pass the bill tonight even if we wanted to because, as I hardly need to say, there have been a number of amendments and when that is the case it is against the rules to have third reading unless there is unanimous consent to it. So the hon. gentleman does not need to worry; this bill cannot possibly be passed tonight. All we are asking is to conclude the committee stage of the bill.
With regard to the other point raised by the hon. gentleman, what I said was that I did not think we should rely upon what we read in the newspapers, but that I would do my best to see that an approach is made to the premier of Quebec to find out whether he would be agreeable to our tabling this correspondence.
